stimulate

STIM-yuh-layt — contains 'stimulus,' something that triggers action; to stimulate is to provide that trigger. · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To stimulate is to rouse or encourage action, growth, or development that already exists or is naturally ready to happen.

The museum's new hands-on exhibits were designed to stimulate children's curiosity about science.

Example

A teacher notices her students growing bored during a lecture, so she switches to a hands-on experiment. Within minutes, hands are raised everywhere, and students who were silent moments before are eagerly asking questions.

Rousing curiosity the students already had — they were able to ask questions all along; they just needed a push — is exactly what it means to stimulate something. Unlike 'kindle,' which means igniting an interest where there was none at all, to stimulate means waking up and encouraging energy, interest, or growth that is already there.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

boost: To boost is to increase or improve something that is already measurable — sales, confidence, a signal. To stimulate is to wake activity up: it rouses energy, interest, or growth that is present but idle, setting things moving rather than just adding more.

trigger: To trigger is to set something off — one event causes another to start, instantly and often accidentally. To stimulate is slower and more supportive: it rouses and feeds action or growth that already exists, the way a good question stirs a quiet class to life.

kindle: To kindle is to ignite an interest or feeling where there was none before — striking the first spark. To stimulate is to fan a spark that already exists: it rouses energy, curiosity, or growth that is already there, waiting for a push.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

suppress: to prevent something from happening or growing

discourage: to make something less likely to happen

Where it sits · how powerfully new activity is set off — encourage → stimulate → ignite

encourage vs. stimulate: Encourage is a plainer, weaker word than stimulate — encouraging just offers support, while stimulating actively triggers new growth or activity.

ignite vs. stimulate: Ignite can feel even more powerful than stimulate: to stimulate is to spark growth or interest, but to ignite means to set off something sudden, intense, and hard to stop.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — -stimul-

root — -stimul-: goad, prod (Latin)

suffix — -ate

suffix — -ate: to make or do (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Latin stimulare comes from stimulus, a pointed stick used to drive animals forward. To stimulate something is, at its root, to goad or prod it into new activity.

Use the root in a new word: stimulus

Use the root in a new word: stimulus: A loud noise can act as a stimulus that makes a sleeping cat instantly jump up.
